description:
We are a team of six third-year university students passionate about Data Science, AI, and solving real-world challenges. Our skills include Python, Data Analysis, Data Visualization, basic Machine Learning, and Cybersecurity.

For NASA Space Apps 2026, we aim to transform NASA Earth science data into meaningful insights through creative, interactive, and scientifically reliable solutions. We believe in teamwork, innovation, and making scientific knowledge accessible to everyone.
summary:
EarthLens: Urban Growth Detective
EarthLens measures how fast eastern Greater Cairo (New Cairo and the desert corridor toward Suez, about 1,067 km²) is expanding, and whether that trend is statistically real. We built a pipeline on Google Dynamic World and Sentinel-2 satellite data from 2016 to 2025. It removes the strong seasonal cycle, which swings monthly built-up area far more than the real trend does, and then tests the trend with Kendall and Theil-Sen methods. The result is about +8.6 km² of built-up area per year (95% CI 7.6 to 9.7). We screened out low-quality observations to check the result holds, traced what land the city grew onto (mostly bare desert), and compared the trend with NASA night-time lights, which point the same way. The findings are in a Streamlit app, an HTML dashboard and a Power BI dashboard. The work matters because rapid urban growth strains water, energy and transport, and planners need evidence of how fast it is happening and how reliable the numbers are.
details:
EarthLens measures how fast eastern Greater Cairo (about 1,067 km², New Cairo and the desert corridor toward Suez) is expanding, and whether that growth is statistically real. A Google Earth Engine script pulls Google Dynamic World and Sentinel-2 data for 2016 to 2025 and exports monthly, annual and land-conversion tables. A Python pipeline then removes the seasonal cycle with STL decomposition. It tests the trend with exact Kendall and Theil-Sen methods and a year-block permutation test, and it screens out low-coverage months. It finds what land became built-up and cross-checks the trend against NASA night-time lights. A machine-learning model estimates which areas are most at risk of future conversion. The result is about +8.6 km² of built-up area per year (95% CI 7.6 to 9.7).

Benefits and intended impact

Instead of a raw, noisy chart, planners get a growth rate with a confidence range, and a clear account of how reliable it is. We want evidence of urban expansion to be trustworthy and easy to inspect. Pointing the same pipeline at a different polygon should make it reusable for other cities.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: Google Earth Engine (JavaScript), Dynamic World V1, Sentinel-2 SR Harmonized, NASA VIIRS Black Marble
  • Analysis: Python with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn and matplotlib, plus Jupyter
  • Apps and dashboards: Streamlit and Plotly, a standalone HTML/JavaScript dashboard, and a Power BI version
  • Collaboration: GitHub
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops. The heavy satellite processing ran in Earth Engine’s cloud.

What is creative

  • We treat seasonality as the central trap: monthly built-up area swings about 3x within a year, far more than the decade’s trend, so we measure it carefully instead of trusting the raw series.
  • Conversion counts only land that became built and stayed built two years later, which cuts out one-off blips.
  • We use an independent NASA night-lights dataset as a cross-check.
  • The same findings are offered as a Streamlit app (with a what-if tool), an HTML dashboard and a Power BI dashboard, so each audience gets a format they can use.

Factors we considered

  • Seasonality: the strong seasonal swing could be mistaken for real change.
  • Data quality: we screened months with low coverage or few satellite images.
  • Short series: with only 9 annual points, we report the slope and its confidence interval instead of relying on the Kendall correlation alone.
  • Model-derived data: built-up area is a Dynamic World estimate, not a ground survey.
  • Independence: night lights measure lighting, not buildings, so we treat them as a consistency check. The prediction model learns Dynamic World’s own labels, so we don’t claim its accuracy is independent proof.
  • Reproducibility: we documented the data source, thresholds and study area, and we state the limitations openly.
